about: Justification trainer prompts for Unit 7 (docs/apcalc-architecture.md, "Justification trainer"). Every number is recomputed in scripts/lib/apcalc-exams.mjs (JUSTIFY_NUMBERS).

prompts.title: Checking a solution of a differential equation
prompts.prompt: Show that $y = 4 + 2e^{-3x}$ is a solution of the differential equation.
checklist: Concludes the two sides are equal for every $x$

earns.answer: For $y = 4 + 2e^{-3x}$, the left side is $\frac{dy}{dx} = -6e^{-3x}$. The right side is $-3(y - 4) = -3\left(4 + 2e^{-3x} - 4\right) = -6e^{-3x}$. The two sides are equal for all $x$, so $y = 4 + 2e^{-3x}$ is a solution.
earns.why: It works each side on its own and shows they match for every $x$, not just at one point.

misses.answer: At $x = 0$, $y = 6$ and $\frac{dy}{dx} = -6$, and $-3(6 - 4) = -6$, so it works.
misses.why: Checking one point does not show the function solves the equation; it must hold for every $x$.

prompts.title: Separation with the initial condition
checklist: Uses the initial condition right away: $\frac{9}{2} = 0 + C$, so $C = \frac{9}{2}$
Solves with the positive root, since $y(0) = 3 > 0$: $y = \sqrt{2x^2 + 9}$

earns.why: The constant appears when the antiderivatives are taken and is found from the initial condition before solving for $y$; the sign of the root is chosen from $y(0)$.

misses.answer: $\frac{y^2}{2} = x^2$, so $y = \sqrt{2}\,x$, and adding $C$ with $y(0) = 3$ gives $y = \sqrt{2}\,x + 3$.
misses.why: The constant must be added when you antidifferentiate, not after solving for $y$. Added at the end, it gives a function that does not solve the equation.

prompts.title: Tangent line estimate from a differential equation
prompts.context: The function $y = f(x)$ solves $\frac{dy}{dx} = x - y$ with $f(1) = 3$. The line tangent to its graph at $x = 1$ gives $f(1.2) \approx 3 + (-2)(0.2) = 2.6$.
prompts.prompt: Is $2.6$ an overestimate or an underestimate of $f(1.2)$? Justify your answer with $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$.
checklist: Differentiates with the chain rule on $y$: $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 1 - \frac{dy}{dx}$
Concludes the graph is concave up near $x = 1$, so the tangent line lies below it: an underestimate

earns.answer: $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{d}{dx}(x - y) = 1 - \frac{dy}{dx} = 1 - (x - y)$. At $(1, 3)$ this is $1 - (1 - 3) = 3 > 0$, so the graph of $f$ is concave up near $x = 1$ and lies above its tangent line. The estimate 2.6 is an underestimate.
earns.why: It finds $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ with $y$ treated as a function of $x$, evaluates it at the point, and ties concavity to the position of the tangent line.

misses.answer: $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 1$, which is positive, so the graph is concave up and 2.6 is an underestimate.
misses.why: The conclusion is right but the second derivative is not: differentiating $-y$ gives $-\frac{dy}{dx}$, not 0. A wrong $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ earns neither point.

prompts.title: A maximum read from the differential equation
prompts.context: The function $y = f(x)$ solves $\frac{dy}{dx} = (3 - x)y$, and $f(x) > 0$ for all $x$.
prompts.prompt: Does $f$ have a relative maximum, a relative minimum or neither at $x = 3$? Justify your answer.
checklist: Uses $y > 0$: the sign of $\frac{dy}{dx}$ is the sign of $3 - x$
Says $\frac{dy}{dx}$ changes from positive to negative at $x = 3$, so $f$ has a relative maximum

earns.answer: At $x = 3$, $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$. Because $y = f(x) > 0$, $\frac{dy}{dx} = (3 - x)y$ has the sign of $3 - x$: positive for $x < 3$ and negative for $x > 3$. So $\frac{dy}{dx}$ changes from positive to negative at $x = 3$, and $f$ has a relative maximum there.
earns.why: It uses the given fact $y > 0$ to read the sign of $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and names the derivative that changes sign.

misses.answer: $f$ goes from increasing to decreasing at $x = 3$, so it has a relative maximum.
misses.why: It restates the conclusion. The readers want the reason: $\frac{dy}{dx}$ changes from positive to negative at $x = 3$, which needs $y > 0$.
